R_H1.passageTitle: When a Walk Changes the Ideas

passages.label: A
passages.text: Does walking change cognition during a task? To investigate, Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz decided to conduct a study in which participants generated unusual ideas or tried to arrive at one suitable answer. Their 2014 paper asked whether performance changed after a short period of activity without assuming that creativity was a fixed trait.

passages.label: B
passages.text: In the initial experiment, forty-eight adults worked while sitting and while walking on a treadmill, and one task asked participants to suggest alternate uses for everyday objects that were unusual, appropriate and absent from other participants' responses. The other required one correct word that linked three clues. Walking improved performance on the alternate-uses task for 81 per cent of participants, while only 23 per cent improved on the convergent task. Scores on that focused task were mildly worse during walking, and the result challenges the norm of treating all creative work as one process. More physical stimulation did not simply raise every score. The contrast gave the researchers a useful control within the same broad topic of creative thought.

passages.label: C
passages.text: A second experiment tested whether practice or order could explain the change. Some people sat twice, some sat and then walked, and others walked and then sat. Those who sat after walking still generated more creative uses than people who sat both times, and the short residual effect shows that legs did not have to move at the exact moment an idea appeared. A later repeated-walking condition also showed that the advantage did not simply vanish through repetition, and the researchers contend that a walk immediately before brainstorming can help. They do not tell teams to suppress evaluation forever. Generation may open options, while later judgement helps people arrive at a useful choice.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Later experiments isolated the effects of walking from the characteristics of those surroundings. In the fourth experiment, forty adult participants sat or walked indoors, walked outdoors or were pushed outdoors in a wheelchair. Each person followed a cue to produce analogies. Exposure to changing scenery was one condition to reconstruct in an experiment, because reliance on the outside views alone did not produce the same effect. A thoughtful reader might speculate that navigating indoors could impair this kind of competence, but it did not under the study conditions. An application to people who need to navigate during a work task would require experimental verification. Results did not definitively identify the full causal pathway. Ninety-five per cent of walkers offered at least one novel, high-quality analogy.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Readers can emulate the procedure by walking before an idea session, and the results offer limited grounds to contend that walking helps with all creative work. Taking a walk can change the norm for a meeting, but the measures constrain conclusions about actual inventions. To establish a causal link for a different task, researchers would need a relevant control group and a way to reproduce the result. The implications of increased stimulation differ when participants must suppress unsuitable answers rather than generate alternatives, and the two tasks produced a difference that investigators could not readily attribute to the outdoor setting.

passages.label: A
passages.text: The story of Thomas Edison as a genius who woke himself while drifting off helped inspire Célia Lacaux and colleagues to conduct a study of cognition during N1, the first stage of sleep. The researchers asked whether a short period in this stage would help research subjects arrive at a hidden rule under carefully controlled conditions, with low external stimulation and a task that allowed performance to be measured precisely.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Researchers recruited 109 people, but after six exclusions the analysis included 103 participants in a number-reduction task using strings of eight digits drawn from 1, 4 and 9. Participants learned two rules. When two digits matched, they reported that digit, whereas when the pair differed they reported the remaining digit. A hidden pattern made the second response the final solution. Everyone completed two blocks of thirty trials before the break, and sixteen people who discovered the shortcut during this early phase were excluded from the later comparison because the break could not explain their insight. The remaining participants then completed nine further blocks. An algorithm identified insight from the largest sudden decrease in solving time across the later trials.

passages.label: C
passages.text: During the twenty-minute break, participants rested in a semi-reclined chair in a dark room, with their eyes closed and a bottle in the right hand. They reported their thoughts if it fell. Video polysomnography recorded brain activity, eye movements and muscle activity, allowing researchers to distinguish wakefulness, N1 and the deeper N2 stage without assuming that a falling bottle marked a consistent boundary. Because the comparison relied on naturally occurring differences in sleep stage, physiological classification determined group membership for the analysis. The investigators examined whether the timing and accumulation of brief periods of sleep made a falling object a reliable indicator of the transition. The bottle provided a cue. One application can reconstruct exposure before the competence test. A thoughtful interpretation asks whether reliance on sound can impair classification. Uncertain timing invites researchers to speculate without definitively establishing a boundary.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Spending at least fifteen seconds in N1 was associated with a greater chance of finding the hidden rule. Eighty-three per cent of the N1 group found it, compared with 30 per cent of those who remained awake. The advantage disappeared among participants who reached N2. In a later analysis, the chance of insight was 2.7 times higher after about one minute of N1 than after quiet wakefulness. Medium alpha activity and low delta activity marked the narrow period linked with the best result. Of 63 bottle drops, 26 occurred after N1, and 49 followed accumulated microsleep activity, usually after about one minute, when brief microsleeps were included. The object did not give a perfect indication of the laboratory sleep boundary.

passages.label: E
passages.text: The design constrains the implications, because calling the awake participants a randomly assigned control group and the N1 participants an experimental group would misdescribe how the groups formed. Variation in sleep latency and baseline problem-solving performance could influence how participants were classified and how they performed after the break. The overall difference is therefore one that researchers cannot confidently attribute to sleep alone. To establish a causal link in another setting, they might test a new intervention and try to reproduce the improvement under conditions that also control exposure to stimulation. The study cannot establish that deeper sleep always suppresses creativity or that early-sleep performance reflects a stable trait.

passages.label: A
passages.text: In 2020, researchers investigating creativity used an online practice intervention to conduct a study with 100 undergraduate communication students, and the research subjects completed assessments of performance and beliefs, and the experimental group used game-like exercises, and the control group provided a comparison. The aim was to find out whether guided practice could change aspects of cognition and confidence, rather than simply label some students as naturally creative.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Participants in the practice condition completed ten hours of online work over four weeks. They encountered a defined sequence of challenges without a teacher directing each response, and both groups took the same assessments before and after the practice period. The comparison group did not complete the intervening exercises. Within a challenge, reproducing a displayed pattern can yield a successful response, while producing a workable alternative involves less imitation. This distinction matters because a game can structure the conditions for practice without establishing that every successful action within it demonstrates originality. Giving both groups the same assessments helps distinguish an effect of the practice from a change in how a task is scored, and it also means researchers can ask whether the practice merely makes one type of exercise more familiar or helps a participant respond to a new kind of challenge.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The assessments distinguished four outcomes. One performance score was specific to a field and another assessed performance beyond that field. The researchers separately measured creative self-efficacy, meaning a learner's confidence in their ability to act creatively, and belief in whether creativity could be developed through training. Improved performance need not accompany either belief, since the two judgements concern perceived personal capability and the potential of instruction. Keeping the measures separate makes it possible to describe how the programme affected particular outcomes without treating every change as evidence for the same underlying trait. A learner might solve more of the problems on an assessment while still feeling uncertain about developing a new idea independently. Similarly, believing that creativity can be taught in general is compatible with low confidence in one's own creative work.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Practice improved some measures of performance and confidence. A thoughtful application of the study would distinguish competence on a task from a belief about it. Exposure to each cue in practice can help someone navigate similar exercises. Testing the same way again lets researchers reconstruct what was learned, while reliance on one measure might impair a wider judgement. The team can speculate about longer-term effects, which its available results cannot definitively establish.

passages.label: E
passages.text: The group comparison helps readers arrive at a limited conclusion about the intervention. The setting and short testing period constrain the implications, because success on a task may be different from sustained work elsewhere. Someone who contends that practice changes a stable trait would need different evidence. Researchers could try to reproduce the change with another group, then ask what part of the result they can attribute to a particular exercise and whether they can establish a causal link between that element and a later outcome.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which conclusion did the researchers set out to examine with the two arrangements?
options: Which people could be identified as creative without being assessed
Whether each group could play different games for equal amounts of time
Whether guided practice could affect specific outcomes compared with an arrangement without that practice
Whether every undergraduate had exactly the same beliefs before the intervention

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why were both groups given the same assessments before and afterwards?
options: It makes a difference in results less likely to come from a change in the scoring tasks themselves.
It means the students who did no practice had no need to take a second assessment.
Using the same assessment proves all later gains last indefinitely.
The assessments could measure only how quickly an instruction was read.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why might completing a game challenge successfully be weaker evidence of originality than completing a different task?
options: The group comparison proves every response in a game used a completely different technique.
Completing a familiar pattern proves a learner can invent at any later task.
All alternatives count as copying if the setting is online.
The player could succeed by reproducing a model even though a new task would require creating something less familiar.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which example shows why performance and confidence should be measured separately?
options: Whenever any test score rises the learner automatically becomes confident in their own ideas.
A student can solve more problems but still feel uncertain about starting a new idea without help.
A stronger belief in training establishes equally strong performance in every field.
Confidence should be used instead of measuring what a person can do.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How could a student's two beliefs about creativity differ?
options: A student can believe creativity can be taught and still doubt their own creative ability.
A belief about training always causes students to solve the same number of questions.
Feeling confident means the person must reject teaching as useless.
Only people who cannot do the assessments can hold a belief about training.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What evidence would distinguish a gain on a known type of exercise from applying a skill elsewhere?
options: Compare only how often people opened an exercise they already knew.
Use one practice cue as the measure for every later environment.
Treat a higher score on a familiar task as evidence of performance in another field without testing it.
Compare results on familiar exercises with performance on work that uses different demands or a different context.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What is one reason to try the comparison with a different group?
options: A different group can determine every participant's earlier score without seeing it.
Changing the group removes the need to measure anything separately.
Repeating the study can help check whether the observed change occurs again outside the original group.
A new group guarantees the improvement is a stable personal characteristic.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A researcher claims practice made students' confidence rise because they performed better. What should be checked before accepting that specific link?
options: Use any performance increase to infer the exact confidence change for each student.
Look at the separate confidence results and seek evidence that the performance change caused them.
Treat the two outcomes as one measure so that causes cannot differ.
Conclude that a higher score rules out a change in any belief.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which design would help a team find out whether one part of the practice explains a particular later result?
options: Test the exercise in a comparison that separates it from other activities and measure the stated outcome later.
Use the original set of games unchanged and attribute any result to whichever game was most popular.
Ask whether every learner likes the same game without linking answers to later work.
Remove the comparison group and treat any later skill as a result of the first task.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which conclusion best fits the relationship between the observed improvements and the claims that can be made?
options: When one score rises, both beliefs and creative performance in all fields have changed.
Mixed results show there can be no measure of cognition under controlled practice conditions.
The intervention demonstrates a lifelong change in every participant's personal creative identity.
The practice can improve particular measured results, while effects on long-term or different work need further evidence.
